claims.text: Formation and persistence of a protective oxide above 900 °C is governed by preferential surface segregation of Cr and X.
Cr and X segregation promotes a dense, adherent oxide layer.
The oxide produced through Cr and X segregation has low growth kinetics and high mechanical stability.
The proposed initial material is a single-phase CrFeCoNiX metallic solid solution.
Cr and X interact with oxygen at the surface to form protective oxides.
Cr and X segregate to the surface because of their high affinity for oxygen.
The resulting dense oxide inhibits further oxidation.
The resulting oxide resists mechanical stresses that could cause cracking or spallation.
Increasing Cr and X content will decrease oxide growth rates.
Increasing Cr and X content will improve oxide adhesion.
Si or Al additions will be especially effective at improving protective-oxide behavior.
Lower Cr and X contents will increase susceptibility to oxide cracking and spallation.
Multiphase structures will be more susceptible to oxide cracking and spallation.
CrFeCoNi without an X addition, exposed under the same conditions, is the proposed control baseline.
The hypothesis is bounded to single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloys with X equal to Si, Mn, or Al in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres above 900 °C.
Failure of higher-Cr, higher-X alloys to outperform CrFeCoNi in oxide growth, adhesion, cracking, and spallation would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and boundary require temperatures above 900 °C, but the falsification experiment specifies exposure at exactly 900 °C.

The predicted outcome confidently states that multiphase structures are more susceptible to cracking and spallation, while the stated boundary excludes multiphase alloys and the uncertainty field says their influence remains unclear.
